summary: This work demonstrates on-demand generation and upconversion of itinerant single microwave photons at 8.9 GHz from a superconducting transmon qubit to telecom-wavelength light at 193.4 THz using an electro-optic transducer based on a lithium niobate whispering gallery mode resonator. The transducer operates at exceptionally low added noise of 0.012 quanta and achieves a signal-to-noise ratio of $5.1 	imes$ the measurement uncertainty, enabling quantum networking with superconducting circuits.
motivation: Superconducting qubits require millikelvin operation due to thermal noise swamping the 10 GHz microwave modes at room temperature, creating a fundamental scaling bottleneck for quantum networks. Bridging microwave and optical domains via coherent transduction of non-classical states is essential for distributed quantum technologies, but microwave-to-optical conversion of itinerant non-Gaussian photon states has not been previously demonstrated.
method: A transmon qubit in a 3D aluminum cavity generates single microwave Fock states via blue sideband driving. The itinerant photons propagate through a coaxial cable to an electro-optic transducer consisting of a superconducting microwave cavity with an embedded 2.5 mm radius LiNbO$_3$ disk resonator with thin-film aluminum electrodes. An optical pump at 193.4 THz upconverts the microwave photons via the Pockels effect, and upconverted photons are filtered through four cascaded Fabry-Perot cavities and detected with a superconducting nanowire single-photon detector.
result: Microwave single-photon Fock states with fidelity 97.6% are generated and tomographically reconstructed. Upconverted optical single photons are detected with $	ext{SNR} = 5.1 	imes 10^{0}$ and input-referred added noise $N_{	ext{add}}^{	ext{up}} = 0.012$ quanta at 1 kHz repetition rate, with quantum channel capacity reaching $2.9$ Hz at 20 kHz repetition rate, placing the transducer squarely in the quantum limit ($N_{	ext{add}}^{	ext{up}} < 1$).
